sections.heading: Organization of the Dictionary
sections.summary: Two sections, English-to-Skiri first because most users will not be speakers; entries in both hold the same information.

sections.heading: General Conventions for Citing Skiri Forms
sections.summary: Verbs are cited as uninflected stems, which never occur as words. A stem that needs a preverb (ir-/a-, ut-, uur-) has it in parentheses after the stem, as in tii (ut...); in a word the preverb comes before the stem. A few stems have a zero base, Ø (ut...) 'to be (in a condition)' and Ø (ir...) 'to be one's'; in their non-subordinate forms the vowel of the preverb, or of a subject plural prefix after it, is reduplicated. Nouns are cited in their independent form, with the nominal suffix they need (-uʔ NOM, -hiriʔ INST/LOC, -kat LOC, -ru LOC); the suffix is absent when the noun is incorporated or stands first in a compound. Dependent noun roots (N-DEP), which occur only before another stem, are cited with a final dash (asaa- 'horse; dog', as in asaaki 'dog'). Locatives that occur only in derived forms are also cited with a final dash (iis- 'out of sight'). Other classes are cited in their independent forms.
sections.bears_on: open item 13 (noun possession: the suffix -hiriʔ, and asaaki 'dog' printed here a third time without a final glottal stop)

sections.heading: English-to-Skiri Entries
sections.summary: An entry begins with the English word in bold; each Skiri translation begins a subentry of up to three parts. Part I: the Skiri word or stem in bold; its phonetic form in square brackets, with small bullets between syllables; the class in small capitals, followed by a dash for dependent elements or by the verb class, which rests on the verb's subordinate form; grammatical forms in curly brackets where they are irregular (usually for a dual or plural agent, or the distributive); the English glosses, numbered when there are several, with clarifying phrases in italics; the derivation in angled brackets, with a hyphen between morphemes inside a stem and a plus sign between major constituents, then a literal translation, sometimes with cognates from South Band, Arikara, Kitsai or Wichita. Part II: for verbs the five standard forms; for a dependent form, derived stems that contain it. Part III: cross-references, beginning with 'see', each an English entry head followed by its Skiri equivalent in curly brackets.

quoted.text: (1) first person agent (for active, descriptive, and locative verbs) or first person patient (for passive verbs), in the indicative mode, perfective aspect; (2) third person agent or patient, indicative mode, perfective aspect; (3) third person agent, indicative mode, imperfective aspect; (4) third person agent, gerundial mode (i.e., subordinate absolutive mode), usually perfective aspect; and (5) third person agent, indicative mode, intentive aspect.
Certain verb classes do not allow some of these forms and thus are lacking here.

sections.bears_on: the five verb forms of every entry (form 1 of a passive verb is a first person patient; form 4 is 'usually' perfective); the English index (scripts/repair_english_index.py reads the entries by this structure)

sections.heading: Skiri-to-English Entries
sections.summary: The same structure without subentries. The head is a stem or root for verbs and the independent form for nouns, with a final dash for dependent nouns and locatives. After it come the phonetic form, the class, entry-specific information in curly brackets (grammatical forms for verbs; for most nouns the variant shapes the noun takes when it is incorporated), the glosses and the derivation. Part II holds the same five forms, or derived forms, as in the English section. Figure 6 shows a compound of the zero verb stem with a noun, Ø (ut...) ciksuʔ; such collocations are cited with the verb base first, though the noun may come first in speech.
